issues.legal_issue: A person claiming property through a legatee cannot establish the legatee’s right under an unprobated will when that right is necessary to prove the property title.
material_facts: In a property-title suit, the defendant relied on a will in which the original owner allegedly bequeathed the disputed house to her mother.

The defendant had obtained letters of administration for her mother’s later will, but no probate or letters of administration had been obtained for the earlier will on which the mother’s ownership of the whole house depended.
The defendant could claim the mother’s share as an heir, but establishing the mother’s ownership of the entire house as a legatee depended on the earlier will.
issues.conclusion: The defendant could not establish her mother’s right as a legatee under the unprobated will, and the later letters of administration did not give the defendant title to property that had not belonged to her mother. The bar applied even though the defendant was claiming through the legatee rather than directly as a legatee.
issues.legal_principle: Section 213(1) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 bars the establishment in court of a right as executor or legatee under a will unless probate or letters of administration have been obtained. The bar applies whether the claimant is plaintiff or defendant, and also applies when a person must establish another person’s right as legatee to prove a derivative title. Ghanshamdoss v. Gulab Bi Bai, (1927) I.L.R. 50 Mad. 927, was approved. Probate and administration proceedings address due execution of a will, not title to the property included in it.

predicates.property_title_suit: A party brought a civil suit seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.derivative_title_depends_on_unprobated_w: A party’s claimed title depends on establishing that another person acquired the property as a legatee under a will for which no probate or letters of administration were obtained.
predicates.legatee_right_cannot_be_established: The claimed right as legatee cannot be established in court.

issues.definition: When a property-title suit requires a party to prove another person’s right as a legatee under an unprobated will, that legatee’s right cannot be established.

issues.legal_issue: A decision in probate or letters-of-administration proceedings does not operate as res judicata on a later dispute over title to the property mentioned in the will.
material_facts: The parties had previously litigated applications for letters of administration concerning competing alleged wills that included the disputed house.
A later application for letters of administration was dismissed after the applicant did not appear, and the title to the house was not adjudicated in that proceeding.
The later suit sought a declaration of ownership of the house.
issues.conclusion: The earlier proceedings did not bar the later title claim by res judicata because they had not decided title to the house.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 requires a matter to have been decided in an earlier proceeding for res judicata to apply. Probate and letters-of-administration proceedings determine matters concerning the will, including its due execution, and do not determine title to property. A dismissal following nonappearance, without adjudication of title, therefore did not bar the later title suit.

predicates.later_property_title_suit: A party brought a later civil suit asserting title to property.
predicates.earlier_probate_proceeding: The parties had previously participated in a proceeding concerning probate or letters of administration for a will that included the property.
predicates.title_not_adjudicated_earlier: The earlier proceeding did not decide who owned the property.

issues.definition: A later title claim is not barred by res judicata when an earlier proceeding concerned probate or administration and did not decide ownership of the property.

issues.legal_issue: A party is not estopped from disputing another person’s property title merely because the party previously described the property as belonging to that person in an application for letters of administration.
material_facts: In an application for letters of administration, the claimant described the disputed house as property belonging to her mother.
The other party did not act in reliance on that description.
The parties had separately advanced competing claims based on alleged wills.
issues.conclusion: No estoppel arose because the other party had not acted on the claimant’s earlier description of the house as her mother’s property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 provides for estoppel when a person intentionally causes or permits another to believe a thing to be true and that other person acts on that belief. A prior statement about ownership, without action by the other party on the resulting belief, does not create estoppel.

rule.if: property_title_dispute and prior_property_representation and (not intentional_inducement or not opponent_acted_on_representation)

predicates.property_title_dispute: Parties disputed ownership of property in a legal proceeding.
predicates.prior_property_representation: A party had previously represented that the property belonged to another person.
predicates.intentional_inducement: The party intentionally caused or permitted the other person to believe the representation was true.
predicates.opponent_acted_on_representation: The other person acted on the belief created by the representation.

issues.definition: Estoppel does not arise in a property-title dispute if a party’s prior ownership representation was not intentionally used to induce belief or the other party did not act on that belief.
